news.title: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
news.source_text:
Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions
Open Data Breaking Down Privacy Barriers to Pave the Way for AI in Finance
In the financial sector, the utilization of real-world data faces significant constraints due to strict privacy regulations, compliance requirements, and the need for advanced domain expertise. In this context, the development of agentic AI in the financial domain requires synthetic data capable of avoiding the risks of using real data while reflecting demographics, household structures, and asset statuses to reproduce diverse, realistic financial scenarios.
To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset "Nemotron-Personas-Japan." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs, a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer, an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).
This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development. The Nemotron-Personas collection, including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim, enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world.
What’s in the Dataset?
- 9M personas total (1M records x 9 personas each), written in natural Japanese
- 50 fields per record: 9 persona fields, 11 persona attributes, and 30 contextual fields based on official demographic and labor statistics
- ~1.5B tokens total, including ~750M persona tokens
- ~950k unique names
- 1600+ occupation categories reflecting Japan's workforce
- Comprehensive coverage across demographic, regional, asset distribution, and personality trait axes
- Diverse persona types: Occupations, sports, arts, travel, cooking, finance, financial behavior, and financial concerns
- Natural language persona att
news.summary: Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, a million-record synthetic dataset that blends Japanese demographic and financial data to support AI development in finance without real customer data. The dataset, built with NVIDIA’s NeMo tools, offers realistic, privacy-compliant personas for simulations and model evaluation.
news.enterprise_use: Watch for updates on the NeMo Data Designer integration and assess how this synthetic dataset could replace or supplement existing test data in your AI workflows. Incorporating it could reduce compliance risks and accelerate model training, but monitor for licensing and integration compatibility with your current analytics stack.

news.title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
news.source_text:
Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
Higher-Order Pruning of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
Introduction
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.
Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.
Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.
Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.
In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.
Experts don't work alone
In a standard MoE, each layer has experts, and each input token is routed independently to such experts ( is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights for each expert , wherein the experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, . The output of the layer is then , where is the output of expert for token .

The approach achieves higher performance retention than first‑order pruning techniques, especially at aggressive pruning rates.

news.title: Jensen Huang Hired a PR Firm Known for Handling Sex Scandals Last Year
news.summary_raw: The Nvidia CEO began working with consultants from Heller as early as October 2025, around the same time he was first linked to a suspected Chinese spy.
news.source_text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began working with a crisis communications firm known for handling public scandals a year before the CEO admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The firm, Heller, has handled Huang’s behind-the-scenes communications since at least October 2025, according to two sources familiar with the matter.
Risa Heller, the firm’s founder, has built a reputation as a fixer for powerful men facing allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies, according to a 2023 New York Magazine profile. Her past clients and people who have sought her advice include former congressman Anthony Weiner, chef Mario Batali, and writer Jeffrey Toobin. Heller also handles corporate communications and issues unrelated to personal controversies for its clients.
Heller’s public relations consultants were initially believed to be hired for matters related to Huang’s personal life, including his family’s philanthropic endeavors, according to people familiar with the arrangement. The firm frequently communicated with Huang and his daughter Madison, a product marketing director at Nvidia who has become an increasingly prominent figure within the company, sources tell WIRED. It’s not clear whether Heller’s early work with the Huang family involved Huang’s affair.
In 2024, Huang began appearing in public with a woman who goes by Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed, according to The New York Times. Megaspeed was created when it split off from a Chinese gaming and cloud computing firm in 2023, a few months after the US government began restricting exports of advanced semiconductors to China, including those developed by Nvidia. A subsidiary of Megaspeed later became a major buyer of Nvidia chips.
In early October 2025, Jensen Huang’s business dealings with Megaspeed and his connection to Alice became public in a lengthy New York Times report, which alleged that the US Commerce Department was investigating whether the company was helping Chinese firms evade American export controls through its subsidiaries.
The report caused tensions to rise within Nvidia’s top ranks, and Jensen was rankled by the story, according to sources. By the end of that month, Nvidia’s internal communications teams had been instructed to include Heller’s firm on any press inquiries about Huang, whether personal or professional, according to people familiar with the matter.
When reached by email, a representative for Heller referred WIRED to Nvidia. Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
US intelligence officials have determined that Alice (who has no known relation to Jensen) is a spy working for the Chinese government, according to the Times. Nvidia initially said that Jensen’s interactions with Alice were part of routine business with clients. But on Sunday, Huang acknowledged that his relationship with her was romantic in nature. news.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has engaged Heller, a crisis communications firm known for handling high-profile scandals, to manage both his personal controversies and corporate communications. The firm has been involved since at least October 2025, amid allegations of Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy and potential export control violations involving Nvidia’s chip sales.

news.title: Authors Can Defend Against AI Allegations With ‘Paper Trail’ Tools. Is It Enough?
news.summary_raw: As the publishing industry wrestles with paranoia over the provenance of manuscripts, writers are caught in an impossible bind.
news.source_text:
Andrea Bartz is a prolific novelist with an impressive résumé. Since 2019, she has published five thrillers, become a New York Times bestselling author, had her work optioned by the likes of Netflix and Hulu, and picked up an endorsement from Reese Witherspoon’s influential book club.
She also has a legal claim to fame: Bartz was the lead plaintiff in a class-action suit against Anthropic that alleged the company had downloaded millions of copyrighted books from pirate sites to use as training data for its models. Anthropic last year agreed to pay $1.5 billion in the largest copyright settlement in US history.
But while Bartz and many other writers were on guard against this plunder of their work, another AI threat was brewing. What happens when authors are accused of relying on artificial intelligence themselves?
This past March, the publishing industry found out: Following widespread speculation on social media that a horror novel titled Shy Girl was largely AI-generated, and a Times article about those claims, Hachette Book Group canceled an upcoming US publication run for the novel and discontinued it in the UK, where it had already been released. According to Pangram, a robust but by no means infallible AI detection tool, some 78 percent of the text was AI-generated.
Mia Ballard, the author of Shy Girl, has denied allegations that she used AI to write the novel, claiming that an editor was responsible for AI-assisted changes to a previously self-published version of the book. She has also said that she is pursuing legal action. Since that scandal broke, several more fiction authors have run afoul of AI suspicions, one after winning a short story prize, another after publishers bid into the millions for his crime novel. Both have denied these allegations as well.
But Bartz notes that once the accusations start, the damage is done. As the Shy Girl scandal erupted, she says, “I kind of immediately felt like this was going to lead to a potential witch hunt.” The unavoidable emergence of AI in publishing, she explains, will “have the unintended effect of leading anyone to be able to accuse anyone of using AI,” and at the moment, authors have little recourse in defending themselves against these charges. “There’s no agreed upon standard,” Bartz says, in proving human authorship.
The developers of a host of new software tools hope to change that. Platforms including Workings, Blindproof, Wintertext, Human Ink, and ObraVera promise the means to track and document an author’s writing process, in some cases encrypting and fingerprinting the written work or typing rhythms with unique codes, in order to produce a record of authorship (whether entirely human or AI-assisted). The idea is not just to create a paper trail that writers can point to if someone questions whether they used an LLM but to demonstrate provenance when, for example, text is scraped into AI training sets without attribution or other identifying metadata.

news.summary: Authors now have a suite of AI‑tracking tools—Workings, Blindproof, Wintertext, Human Ink, and ObraVera—to document their writing process and establish provenance. These tools aim to help writers defend against accusations that they used LLMs, a growing concern as publishers and courts grapple with AI‑authorship claims.

news.title: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny
news.summary_raw: Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy threatens to complicate Nvidia’s lobbying efforts to loosen U.S. chip export restrictions and maintain access to China’s lucrative AI market.
news.source_text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology. The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on the relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday. U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia. Historically, China has been a big market for the company. It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives. In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to expand access to China, and some of his persuasion tactics have been successful. Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.
On numerous occasions, Huang has publicly lamented export controls, calling them a “failure” at a conference last year and saying in May that it was “not wise” for the U.S. and China to create two distinct AI ecosystems. He has also warned that shutting Nvidia out of China’s compute market would enable the country to develop its own AI chips to challenge Nvidia internationally.
China is already moving in that direction. Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China. Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024. At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
Still, the allegations involving Alice Huang open new scrutiny of the company’s business relationships and could taint any assurances Nvidia offers that it can prevent sensitive technology from reaching unauthorized customers.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly warned officials close to Trump earlier this year about Huang’s relationship with an alleged spy. Even if Nvidia’s
news.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a former employee alleged to be a Chinese spy has sparked intense scrutiny over the company’s China business and potential export control violations. The incident could prompt heightened regulatory oversight and impact Nvidia’s ability to supply AI chips to Chinese customers, potentially affecting global AI supply chains.

news.title: Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines
news.summary_raw: Anthropic bought billions of dollars worth of natural gas turbines in a deal that could give it buyer's remorse.
news.source_text:
AI’s power crunch has become so acute that Anthropic, a company that has generally avoided buying physical infrastructure, is spending $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines.
The AI company, which is planning to go public this year, is buying Caterpillar generators that equipment supplier OnePWR had originally ordered, according to a Financial Times report. The generators are capable of producing up to 1.7 gigawatts of electricity.
Historically, Anthropic has preferred to rent rather than buy. The company disclosed in its S-1 filing in May that it is paying SpaceX subsidiary xAI $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 to use xAI’s computing power.
“We expect to enter into additional similar services contracts,” Anthropic stated in the filing, meaning more deals to rent computing power.
But as demand for compute ramps up, the market for power has also grown increasingly uncertain, which may have forced its hand. The backlog for natural gas turbines stretches into the early 2030s, and queues to connect to the electrical grid can be just as long.
Anthropic’s purchase looks like a last resort.
According to the report, OnePWR ordered the turbines a couple years ago, but couldn’t find financing to complete the purchase. Anthropic had planned to buy them from OnePWR but instead went directly to Caterpillar, the manufacturer.
It’s not clear why OnePWR was unable to secure financing despite Anthropic’s apparent interest as a customer. Whatever the case, Anthropic likely wanted to keep the generating capacity to itself rather than give a competitor an opportunity to snap it up.
AI companies have been ramping up their purchases of natural gas equipment and supplies in recent years. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta have all announced plans to build massive natural gas power plants to power their data centers on site, rather than drawing from the public grid.
The binge has given a second wind to fracking, the drilling method used to extract natural gas from underground rock. And if the buildout proceeds as planned, U.S. data centers alone could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035. The reliance on natural gas also exposes hyperscalers to price fluctuations. One analyst expects that prices could more than triple by the end of the decade in some markets. If that happens, Anthropic might have a serious case of buyer’s remorse.
news.summary: Anthropic has announced a $3.4 billion purchase of natural‑gas turbines to secure its own power supply as AI compute demands surge. The move underscores a growing trend of hyperscalers building on‑premise energy infrastructure to avoid grid volatility and cost spikes.
news.enterprise_use: Monitor Anthropic’s strategy as a bell‑wether for the broader AI industry’s power needs. Consider evaluating your own data center energy sourcing or contingency plans for rising natural‑gas prices, especially if your organization plans large‑scale AI workloads.

Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy
The new system will enable participating financial service providers to clear and settle payments in real time, providing a made-in-Canada platform for future innovation and prosperity.
OTTAWA, ON, November 9, 2026 – Payments Canada today announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR). This new national payment system will transform day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by enabling instant speed and settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility and data-rich messaging through existing banking and payment channels.
The launch of Canada’s RTR marks a major milestone in modernizing the critical infrastructure that underpins Canada’s economy and future growth. The RTR will enable participating members, including financial institutions, credit unions and payment service providers, to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time for their customers, 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
“A stronger, more productive economy relies on modern financial infrastructure that can match our ambition,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail lays the foundation for a more dynamic and competitive digital economy, driving innovation, expanding choice and creating new opportunities for Canadians while positioning our country for long-term growth.”
“The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” said Susan E. Hawkins, President and CEO, Payments Canada. “As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the RTR gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on. By collectively leveraging this rail, our ecosystem will unleash its full potential, enabling our members to build capabilities that drive innovation, resilience and growth for businesses and consumers across the nation.”
Ron Morrow, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne and Susan E. Hawkins
The RTR will drive significant cost savings and economic growth in Canada over the next decade. The C.D. Howe Institute projects that, with its functionalities at launch, the RTR will generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient). Extending beyond these cost savings, the RTR is expected to generate $16 billion in economic gains, growing to $27 billion as new functionalities are introduced over time.
“The Real-Time Rail is an important step in modernizing Canada's payment infrastructure and ensuring it keeps pace with Canadians' evolving needs,” said Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. “The Bank will oversee the system so that it operates safely and reliably while ensuring Canadians can benefit from innovations in financial services.”

news.title: After the midterms, things are looking rocky for Elon Musk and data centers
news.summary_raw: On Equity, we unpacked what the midterms mean for the tech industry.
news.source_text:
Democrats’ historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could also have a dramatic effect on the tech industry.
In dozens of local ballot measures, voters rejected data centers. And even when they weren’t voting on the issue directly, they were electing politicians — like Texas’ new governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned on the promise of restricting data centers.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry. Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.”
And Kirsten said that while data centers probably weren’t the main cause of the “blue wave,” they’ve become an “an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about” getting their projects approved. And now, “we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, ‘Actually, we can change our policies.’”
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. news.title: GitHub New pull request overview page in public preview
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://github.blog/changelog/2026-11-05-new-pull-request-overview-page-in-public-preview/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50408931
Points: 150
# Comments: 101
news.source_text:
New pull request overview page in public preview
On a long pull request, checking what’s blocking often means scrolling past dozens of comments and timeline events just to reach the merge box. And once you’re there, you still need to work out what to do next. As people need to review more and more pull requests, time spent scrolling adds up. So we’ve begun to rethink the entire experience, beginning with addressing a familiar challenge: finding what’s blocking progress and determining what to do next.
Today, we’re introducing the Overview page as an opt-in public preview, with rollout continuing through the weekend. It brings merge status and next available actions to the top of the page in a compact readiness summary. It’s the first step toward making pull requests easier to follow as code, conversations, and reviews evolve.
The merge box, distilled
We’re starting with the merge box, the place developers go to see whether a pull request can move forward. Rather than just moving it higher, we’ve also redesigned it to show the same information in less than half the space.
- Explore the supporting signals: A compact view of checks, comments, and approvals keeps the context nearby without making every detail compete for attention.
- Address what’s blocking: Take action to move the pull request forward, such as updating your branch.
- See if it’s ready to merge: Check merge readiness and merge when requirements are met.
Start with the summary, then follow the detail that matters to your next step (e.g., get to failing checks, see who still needs to approve, or open the relevant comments).
Keep your place. Focus your attention.
This first preview also introduces more ways to catch up on activity and focus the conversation so you can spend less time finding your place.
- Narrow the conversation: Filter for unresolved conversations or comments you wrote to find open questions or follow up on your feedback.
- Read the latest comments first: Sort comments from newest to oldest instead of starting with the earliest discussion.
- Catch up on activity: Use the summary in the upper-right to find review comments, review requests, and other updates.
You can also mark a draft ready for review or close a pull request from the header, with available actions depending on your permissions.
Try the new overview
To join, select the ✨ Try the Overview page button in the header. We’re opening this preview early so you can try the new direction on your own pull requests and help shape what comes next. You can use the same menu to return to the classic overview during the preview.
Help shape what comes next
This preview is very much a starting point, not the finished pull request experience. Try it on your next pull request. What is easier to find? Where do you still lose context? What sends you back to the classic overview?
Share your feedback and report issues in the overview preview feedback discussion.
news.summary: GitHub has launched a new pull request overview page in public preview, placing merge status and actionable next steps at the top of the page to reduce scrolling and improve review efficiency. The feature also introduces compact views of checks, comments, and approvals, along with filters to focus on unresolved discussions and recent activity.
news.enterprise_use: S1: Visit GitHub, enable the Overview page for your repositories this week and test the new merge status panel. S2: Without adopting it, reviewers may continue to spend excessive time scrolling through long PRs, slowing deployment pipelines and increasing error risk. news.title: Physicl raises $10M to make the digital world real enough for robots
news.summary_raw: Physicl is trying to solve the sim-to-real gap with a pipeline originally built to market goods online.
news.source_text:
Alex de Vigan’s last business got swamped by the rise of generative AI, but now he’s betting the tech that team had built, a platform for creating tempting product renderings for e-commerce, can be re-purposed to make robots more useful.
His new venture, Physicl, has raised $10 million in seed funding led by Inovia Capital to help world model designers and robot builders solve thorny training problems with more realistic simulations.
Founder and CEO de Vigan spent the last decade building nfinite, which made it easy for brands and retailers to create 3D models of their goods and display them online. The arrival of transformer-based AI models led that company to focus more on generative imagery, but de Vigan saw a new purpose for his team and the tech stack they’d built to faithfully render 3D environments.
“What we were super unique about doing in 3D, AI was going to replace, but something was missing in AI: its ability to understand, interact, and manipulate space and objects,” de Vigan says.
Researchers developing physical AI models to make robots more capable of tasks like handling diverse, small objects have been frustrated by the returns of training them on video, and the expense of gathering data through remote operations.
Simulations in digital worlds are seen as a promising solution, but ensuring that these simulated worlds are faithful to real-world physics has proven difficult. De Vigan believes that the pipeline his previous company built to “transform unstructured, incomplete, heterogeneous real-world information into a high-fidelity physical representation… with correct geometry, materials, and physics” can now be used to make physical AI models more effective.
Physicl is entering a crowded category of startups vying to provide data and tooling to foundation model builders and robot operators. “The space is very young and very blurry sometimes,” de Vigan admits. There are a variety of companies collecting, labeling, or generating data in different modalities as their customers try to figure out the secret sauce that will make robots live up to their promise.
In particular, Physicl wants to focus on post-training models on difficult edge cases. The startup is releasing a product called Studio with 10,000 3D environments and 100,000 assets that represent various objects. It lets users create scenes to generate synthetic data for training robots on specific problems. For example, Studio could be used to generate training data to help a robot that has trouble discerning a cup on a cluttered counter-top, or while the cup is in shadow.
SpAItial, a world model builder, collaborated with Physicl as an early customer to improve the fidelity of its products, the latest of which, Echo-3, was released last week. news.title: Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy AI agent security startup Clutch for $500M
news.summary_raw: Clutch, backed by Lightspeed and SignalFire, was last valued at $85 million, according to a source.
news.source_text:
Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security, a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source. The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.
Palo Alto Networks and Clutch Security did not respond to a request for comment. The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.
The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily. Upwind, a startup using AI to secure cloud infrastructure, recently turned down an acquisition offer from Datadog that valued it at roughly 40 times ARR, TechCrunch reported last week.
If the deal happens, it would be Palo Alto Networks’ seventh acquisition this year, according to PitchBook. The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.
In September, Palo Alto Networks acquired Console, a two-year-old startup that uses AI agents to automate routine IT help desk tasks. The transaction valued Console at $500 million in stock and cash, TechCrunch reported. Other VC-backed companies that Palo Alto Networks has scooped up this year include NEA-backed Embrace, for $325 million; Chronosphere, an observability platform backed by Greylock and Lux Capital, for $2.95 billion; and Koi, a cyber startup backed by Battery and Team8, for $231 million, according to regulatory filings.
Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired. Cyera, a cybersecurity startup valued at $12 billion earlier this year, acquired Oasis Security, which, like Clutch, focuses on managing AI agents’ access to systems, for $1 billion. Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million, Calcalist reported.

The deal would bring Clutch’s agent‑access controls into Palo Alto’s portfolio, potentially reshaping how enterprises secure AI‑powered workflows.

news.title: Nvidia will investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy
news.summary_raw: In a memo to the company, Huang admitted that he had an affair.
news.source_text:
Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation.
Nvidia also published a message that Huang sent to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed (though he didn’t mention her by name). A memo circulating among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Huang added that he’d “fallen short” of his responsibility to the company.
“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said.
As the AI race between the United States and China heats up, chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus. Huang also seems to have a close relationship with President Donald Trump, who’s been a cheerleader of the AI (or “superintelligence”) industry.
In its announcement, Nvidia’s board said that it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or company secrets were compromised. It also said that Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” and that the board has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”
The investigation will be conducted by independent directors working with outside legal counsel.
In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers.
Other companies involved in the AI boom have warned employees to be wary of possible spies, including those offering sex or romance.
news.summary: Nvidia’s board has launched an independent probe into CEO Jensen Huang after reports he was targeted by a Chinese spy operation. The investigation focuses on potential security breaches and corporate integrity, with the board stating no evidence of compromised secrets so far.

Failure to do so could expose your IT environment to undiscovered vulnerabilities in critical AI infrastructure. The most affected tool is your GPU deployment strategy within your AI workloads.

Every Mac since macOS 13 (2022) ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about who you are, who you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, what you do and when. In this post, we look into how this system works and give you a tool to peek into your own graph.
The position
A family fork: one knight on e2 attacks White's king, queen, rook and bishop at once. White's pieces are the household the graph is about; the knight is the store, one move from every one of them. White's own last move, 18.e3, emptied the square it stands on. White is in check and has one legal reply, Kh1; then the knight takes the queen. The check falls on the one who accepted the terms. What is lost is someone else.

Finding
Target
Apple Intelligence / Personal Knowledge Graph
Affected
macOS 13+, Intel and Apple silicon
Class
Privacy Personalized AI
What if I told you that every Mac since 2022 ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about you and the people around you: who you are, who you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, with whom, what you do and when. This graph is built on device by cross-referencing pretty much everything on the machine: Contacts, Calendar, Photos, Messages, Mail, location, Screen Time and a long tail of behavioral signals. And, more importantly, it is held as a queryable store that LLMs retrieve from (allegedly). Would you believe me?
Well, that's what is happening, and interestingly enough, there is little documentation of how this whole mechanism works on your Mac. The closest thing to an official description is the man page (man 8 knowledgeconstructiond), and this is all you get:
Previous work: To be fair, Apple's own researchers did publish a paper on the techniques behind this graph construction, back in 2023. But there is next to nothing on how it is integrated into macOS: which versions run it, and the exact list of what is collected and inferred. And not a word about the "kinship" inference discussed below. Also, we personally ran into it while doing some security research on the Apple Intelligence bundle in macOS 26 in August 2026; but a few months before, Nic Lydon came across the same database and wrote it up in I Built a Personal Knowledge Graph. Apple Had Already Built One on My Laptop.
But we go a bit deeper.
This blog post is an account of some analysis work we carried out on what the knowledge graph actually does, so that you (the user) can get a better understanding of how this mechanism works, and some clarity on what the graph holds about you and your family and friends. Everything in it was collected on macOS 26 (26.6.2 at the time of writing).
To this end, we open-source a local dashboard (iKnow) you can use to read the content of your personal knowledge graph on your Mac.
Finall

news.title: Franklin Templeton uses OpenAI to support investment research
news.summary_raw: Starting with equity research, Franklin Templeton is developing AI workflows to help portfolio managers compare research views and examine investment risks.
news.source_text:
Franklin Templeton uses OpenAI to support investment research
Starting with equity research, Franklin Templeton is developing AI workflows to help portfolio managers compare views and examine risks.
Franklin Templeton wants AI to help portfolio managers examine different research views and the risks behind an investment idea. Codex is one of several tools our investment teams are using to develop workflows for investment research.
“The biggest unlock from using OpenAI’s tools is the ability to merge continuous intelligence with human judgment. It has really transitioned because, beforehand, AI was automating our human-led process. Now AI is actually automating the ability to surface intelligent insights, and that intelligence layer plus human judgment is just a fantastic unlock.”
When Franklin Templeton first tried using AI, the team put data in a database and connected the models to it. But it didn’t produce the answers the teams needed because the models didn’t understand how the data fit together. When the team added agents and a semantic layer, a structured model of what the firm’s data means and how it’s connected, the results changed. The team is using Codex and other tools to develop this connected intelligence layer. "We've been able to build what we think of as a connected intelligence layer," Dudley says. "We're bringing the data into the tools, and we're surfacing insights that make a difference."
Research, risk, compliance, and trading offer different perspectives on an investment. Franklin Templeton’s ambition is to bring those inputs together for portfolio managers. “We're able to bring that all in and then use that to surface insights to the people who are making decisions, which are our portfolio managers,” Dudley says.
Dudley describes the earlier equity-research workflow as human-led and sequential: an analyst performs first-pass stock analysis, reviews earnings calls, and studies competitors in each business line. The goal is to surface useful information as analysts prepare new ideas to be pitched to portfolio managers or provide updates on existing positions in the portfolio. As she puts it, “It's just continuous intelligence combined with that human judgment.”
In the workflow Franklin Templeton envisions, its investment teams will have access to a governed, reusable intelligence foundation that brings together trusted connectors, portfolio and workflow context, and agentic capabilities that surface actionable insights for its analysts and portfolio managers.
Franklin Templeton has used Codex in hackathons, bringing experts alongside investment practitioners as they develop their own tools. Its Investment AI champions are working to turn experiments into production-ready workflows, with security review, expert support, and data controls as part of that process.
Dudley says, “We have moved from augmenting our research process to reimagining the investment research workflow.”

news.title: Apps for Caregivers Get a Dose of AI, but That Might Not Be Enough
news.summary_raw: The apps and platforms that help family caregivers manage their loved ones’ needs are becoming more capable, but the broader issue of caregivers’ well-being remains unsolved.
news.source_text:
My husband and I are caregivers for our middle son, who has multiple disabilities and requires full-time support. We do our best to keep one another up to date on the activities that fill his daily life while also managing his numerous medical specialists, procedures, and therapies. We have to stay in constant communication while also working our jobs, caring for three teenagers, and managing a household. It’s tough.
We’re not alone in our struggles. According to AARP, in 2025, an estimated 63 million Americans cared for adults or children with a medical condition or disability. On average, these caregivers spend up to 27 hours per week providing care.
This caregiver crisis, where so many Americans provide ongoing, complex care and, as a result, endure poor health, financial strain, and isolation, is worsening as caregivers need more support and better systems.
Helpfully, to lighten the mental load, caregiver apps are aimed at families who are supporting seniors, children, or anyone with a diagnosis that needs regular management.
Apps for Different Types of Caregivers
Every caregiver’s situation is different, and the apps and programs in this space reflect a diversity of needs.
Medisafe, which was created in 2013, tracks medications and sends reminders so users don’t miss a dose. The program can also notify a caregiver if a dose is missed. It gives its users the ability to track medical appointments, track their symptoms, and maintain a list of health care contacts and measurements. It also has a drug interaction checker where users can enter multiple medications to see if they are safe to take at the same time.
Caring Village, which was founded in 2015, has an appointment calendar, a to-do list, and a wellness journal where users can keep track of their loved one’s symptoms and moods, and even upload a photo. Caregivers can assign tasks through the app, create a care plan, and receive reminders to take medication. The app also comes with an AI assistant called Julia that can answer caregiving questions.
In 2022, Bret Koncak, based on his experiences with his two sons who have complex needs, cocreated Mejo, a web-based caregiver app. Users enter an individual’s medical history, which is then consolidated into a one-page summary that can be shared with caregivers, doctors, and therapists.
“A lot of people think that caregiving begins and ends with interactions with the health care system, but a lot of it is about what happens between care visits,” says Koncak. “That's what we're focused on.” For $6 a month or $60 a year, the premium version of Mejo gives users access to daily journaling, which they can share with other caregivers, so everyone stays on the same page without having to catch up verbally.

news.title: Crusoe sells troubled Wyoming data center project to Google
news.summary_raw: The deal highlights the challenges of developing massive AI data centers.
news.source_text:
Crusoe, an eight-year-old, Denver-based data center developer recently valued at $30.9 billion, confirmed Friday it has sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google.
Google, which Crusoe had tried and failed to land as a customer for the project, is taking over the development after reportedly raising concerns about its cost and construction timeline under Crusoe’s management.
Crusoe initially announced the project last year with Blackstone-backed infrastructure company Tallgrass, planning to eventually scale it to 10 gigawatts of power capacity.
Google did not disclose how much it paid Crusoe for the unfinished project, but it announced plans to invest $17 billion to develop the data center campus.
The deal highlights how difficult it can be for independent data center developers to deliver massive projects on time and within budget, given the challenges of securing equipment and power. Growing opposition from local communities can further complicate development.
Despite taking over the Wyoming facility, Google hasn’t walked away from working with Crusoe entirely. Crusoe is developing another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas.
The deal to sell the site to Google was first reported by Bloomberg in June, but the Wyoming setback didn’t stop Crusoe from raising a $3.9 billion round in September.
Crusoe makes money by leasing data center space to customers that bring their own GPUs, by renting out its own GPUs, and by selling compute power used to run AI models, known as inference.
Crusoe’s largest projects serve some of the biggest names in AI. Its campus in Abilene, Texas, is being built in phases for Oracle and OpenAI, and the company is also constructing a separate 900-megawatt campus next door for Microsoft, with its first building expected to come online in mid-2027. Meta is also a customer, and Bloomberg reported that the trading firm Jane Street signed a $13 billion, five-year cloud deal with Crusoe.
Crusoe was founded by Chase Lochmiller, now its CEO, and Cully Cavness, who started it as a cryptocurrency-mining business powered by natural gas that would otherwise have been burned off. In September, alongside its $3.9 billion funding round, the company added three board members, including JB Straubel, the Redwood Materials founder and Tesla board member who invested in Crusoe in 2021. Crusoe later became the first customer of Straubel’s energy-storage business.
news.summary: Google has taken over an unfinished Wyoming data center project from Crusoe, investing $17 billion to accelerate its development. This move underscores the challenges independent developers face with cost, timelines, and community opposition while scaling large-scale AI infrastructure.
news.enterprise_use: Monitor Google Cloud’s data‑center expansion plans for potential opportunities or risks in your cloud strategy; consider how increased capacity might affect your tenancy or cost models.

Flipsnack focused its ChatGPT Ads campaigns on getting people to try its product, growing registrations while lowering the cost per signup.
Results at a glance

Connecting a versatile product to a specific need
Flipsnack(opens in a new window) helps teams turn static documents into interactive digital experiences. Its customers use the platform to create product catalogs, sales presentations, brochures, internal communications, and training materials.
For Flipsnack, that range of applications creates a marketing challenge: helping people recognize how the product fits the work they need to do. As the company increased its focus on business customers, it wanted to reach people with needs that its product category alone might not clearly describe.
Flipsnack had relied heavily on search advertising. Its ChatGPT Ads test became an opportunity to learn which customer needs could translate into product signups.
Measuring the action that brings people into the product
Because Flipsnack is a visual product, prospective customers often want to experience it before speaking with sales. Its campaign landing pages directed people into a signup flow, making completed registration the first meaningful step the team could measure and optimize for.
To help business customers see where the product could fit their work, Flipsnack expanded beyond its original, broader Flipbook campaign. Separate campaigns for Magazine, Catalog, and Brochure addressed specific document needs, while campaigns for Sales Enablement, Employee Benefits, Real Estate, and Hospitality connected the product to business applications and industries.
“A sales team and an internal communications team can use the same product for very different jobs. We want our campaigns to help each see where Flipsnack fits.”
Flipsnack’s initial click-focused campaigns brought in traffic and signups. After seeing better delivery and registration efficiency in conversion-focused campaigns, the team rebuilt existing campaigns with a conversions objective and bidding set to maximize conversions.
Improving registration efficiency
Flipsnack created conversion-focused versions of five existing US campaigns that had used a clicks objective with fixed bids.
Early results following the shift to conversion-focused campaigns were encouraging. Across five campaigns, registrations increased approximately 310% while cost per registration fell approximately 75%, with daily budget settings unchanged.1
“What stood out was that we were getting more registrations at a lower cost per signup. That gave us the confidence to make conversion optimization the focus of our campaigns.”

news.title: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO
news.summary_raw: AI usage keeps climbing, but spending has stalled. Price cuts and smarter cost controls among the biggest spenders could challenge investor assumptions about AI hypergrowth.
news.source_text:
Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it.
A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.
As Anthropic gears up for its IPO, the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed.
“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”
Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “AI-pilled” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said.
Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.
“If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.”
“The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued.
October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong.
Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “Cracks in the AI Thesis”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace.
“OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets.
Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market.
Subsidizing use of expensive technology
news.summary: Ramp’s latest report shows AI spending has stalled in late summer, even as token volumes rise, as OpenAI and Anthropic cut prices to keep customers. The slowdown hints that the AI hyper‑growth narrative may be overstated and could impact enterprise budgets for AI tooling.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on your AI budget and vendor pricing; review any current contracts with OpenAI or Anthropic to ensure cost‑efficiency. If you’re using their APIs, verify whether your usage still aligns with budget forecasts, and consider exploring alternative providers or negotiated enterprise discounts to avoid over‑spending. This is a good time to audit AI spend across departments and adjust allocation if necessary.

news.title: Megaspeed exec was recruited to spy on Nvidia CEO, according to US intelligence memo
news.summary_raw: A memo circulated earlier this year reportedly claimed that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited a female technology executive to spy on Nvidia's CEO.
news.source_text:
A memo circulated earlier this year claimed that technology executive Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to multiple media reports.
The New York Times, which had previously said Nvidia’s chief executive had been the target of Chinese intelligence, was the first to report on the memo, which was reportedly based on U.S. intelligence. The Financial Times subsequently reported that the memo also claimed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed.
An Nvidia spokesperson told the NYT that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with its customers.
A separate NYT report examined New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized by the U.S. Commerce Department to buy advanced Nvidia chips. But at the office address listed by New Matrix, reporters only found “a hollow gray shell,” raising concerns that it could be a front for a blacklisted private equity firm.
The Nvidia spokesperson said the company sells “the first, best and most of our technology in America.”
news.summary: A U.S. intelligence memo alleges that a China-linked executive was recruited to surveil Nvidia’s CEO, with potential implications for technology supply chains and insider risk. The claim raises concerns about corporate security and the integrity of vendor relationships.
news.enterprise_use: Review your vendor onboarding and access controls for any companies linked to Megaspeed or New Matrix, and ensure that privileged credentials are monitored for anomalous activity. Failure to do so could expose your organization to supply‑chain or insider threats.

news.title: What I run on my $10 USD OpenStick homelab
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://blog.bosscher.ch/posts/openstick/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50406670
Points: 169
# Comments: 37
news.source_text:
A while ago I bought an OpenStick on a whim for 10 dollars (including shipping!) because it seemed like such a cool novelty piece of hardware.
For 10 dollars you get:
- 512 MB of RAM (~450 MB usable)
- 4x ARM Cortex-A53 CPU cores at 1 GHz
- 4 GB eMMC flash
- 150 Mbit/s Wi-Fi
- 4G modem and GPS
- Passively cooled, so 100% silent!
- 1 programmable LED :)
Now, you might look at this hardware and think “my watch is more powerful than that”, and you wouldn’t necessarily be wrong, but there’s still a lot of fun to be had with a device this size, and it’s a great gadget to get started with self-hosting.
The installation process is a bit involved, but once you’re up and running it runs Debian, which brings all the classic goodies such as systemd (among other things, a scheduler and service monitoring for Linux) and Podman (lightweight containerization). For 10 USD you basically get a home server with minimal power usage and zero noise!
There’s actually a lot of useful software that runs great on this thing. Some of my favorites are:
CastSponsorSkip (5–10 MB)
This is a little service that connects to any running Google Cast device and skips sponsorships (and sometimes ads). It barely uses any resources, and after a while you forget that it exists, but it does make the whole YouTube experience a lot nicer!
AdGuard Home - my own fork (40 MB)
AdGuard Home blocks bad domains at the DNS level: spyware, malware, and so on. These days devices have a tendency to spy on you. Smart TVs run content recognition continuously, washing machines scan your network, and your coffee maker might be spying on you.
A DNS blocker cannot block all bad requests (you’ll need a proper firewall for that), but it sure can block a whole lot. After adding a few blocklists, 60% of my queries are now blocked. Most seem harmless, but I’m pretty sure that some aren’t.
I’m running my own fork, which can handle large blocklists in an efficient manner, but you probably shouldn’t run binaries provided by random strangers, so I’ve also included the link to the official version below (which is totally fine if you limit yourself to smaller blocklists).
AdGuard Home Next-Gen - 40 MB (independent of the size of the blocklist) AdGuard Home - 40 MB (with a small (200k) blocklist)
Zeroclaw (64 MB)
Zeroclaw is an AI agent harness. It supports 30 channels (Telegram, email, WhatsApp, etc.), has sensible security defaults, a nice web UI, and integrations with all the major LLM providers.
I ran OpenClaw for a while on my Kubernetes cluster, but it mostly caused a lot of frustration: it worked, but it used 1 GB+ of memory, broke with every update, and they kept changing functionality in ways that broke my existing workflows. Zeroclaw feels like a breath of fresh air. It uses ~3 MB RSS when idle, covers all the functionality that I need, and the security defaults are sensible and easy enough to disable. The next version will (hopefully!) have rich message support for Telegram, implemented by yours truly. The
news.summary: A $10 OpenStick device can run lightweight Debian with systemd, Podman, and useful services like AdGuard Home and Zeroclaw. The post showcases how low-cost hardware can host DNS filtering and AI agent software for home and small‑office use.
news.enterprise_use: Check whether your organization could deploy a low‑cost ARM device for edge‑network filtering or lightweight AI tooling. If you already run AdGuard Home or a similar DNS blocker, consider a proof‑of‑concept on a few OpenSticks to validate performance and security before scaling.

news.title: After blocking Muse, Amazon now lets users text Alexa to help them shop
news.summary_raw: Amazon said that the feature will roll out to millions of users in coming weeks.
news.source_text:
Amazon is jumping on the currently most popular bandwagon for interacting with AI agents: texting. The company on Friday said it is launching a feature that lets customers chat with its Alexa AI agent over text messages to help them shop, much like you can with AI agents like Muse or Instinct.
The move comes after Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from querying its site in September. The company is rolling the features out just before the start of the holiday shopping season.
The e-commerce giant said select U.S. customers will get a text asking them to enable the shopping feature. Those with access can text Alexa to shop on Amazon using natural language queries, spanning everything from searching for items, adding them to cart, and purchasing.
The text agent builds on the recent shopping-focused upgrades to Alexa, and so can manage lists, keep tabs on prices, search for items across the web, compare products, and check the status of orders. Users can also share a picture of an item or someone wearing an outfit to search for similar listings on Amazon.
The company said over time, Alexa will learn users’ preferences and suggest items accordingly.
The company said users who don’t get invited to use this feature can sign up to a waitlist. The feature will be rolled out more broadly in the coming weeks.
As the market for consumer-focused AI agents balloons, platforms like Amazon are building their own to tap this new avenue of user interaction. Last month, delivery company DoorDash said that third-party agents had so far only placed hundreds of orders in total on its platform, and that it plans to concentrate on developing its own text-based agent, launched in September, further.
news.summary: Amazon has launched a text‑based interface for its Alexa AI shopping agent, allowing users to chat via SMS to search, add to cart, and purchase items. The feature, rolled out ahead of the holiday season, builds on Alexa’s recent shopping upgrades and will be available to select US customers before a broader release.
news.enterprise_use: No direct action required for the IT engineer’s current toolset; monitor for potential future integrations or security implications.

news.title: The end of Microsoft Research's AI Frontiers group
news.summary_raw:

news.source_text:
In 2023 after the ChatGPT release, it was clear to me that research needed to be more organized to succeed than was typical within Microsoft Research. The amount of support and focus which other research groups were applying was great enough that even with a clever idea pursued by one person it was likely to arrive late and unconvincing because one person could not move fast enough and the baselines which one person could assemble just were not strong enough to really show that an idea was worth taking flight. Several other folks thought similarly and we organized to create the AI Frontiers sub-organization within MSR.
In AI Frontiers, we actively tried to organize coherent research efforts. This was not precisely “top down” or “bottom up”, but rather mostly somewhere in the messy middle. There were disagreements of course, and resolving them was sometimes quite challenging. Compute availability was also an often-severe bottleneck. But at a high level I was under the general impression that the organization was succeeding in doing pioneering things, particularly given the small size of AIF (~50 people) and relative to what we could do previously. Much of the work of AIF was figuring out how to make agents work, for example the Autogen orchestration framework and the Fara computer use agent. In NYC however, several of us were interested in developing new fundamental capabilities such as the Next Latent objective which enables extrapolation, Dion3 which creates an optimized/improved Muon, or the Full Bandwidth Transformer which efficiently makes models function substantially more powerfully via recursion.
We also actively tried to share with the rest of MSR. For example, AIF decided to develop a monorepo that was shared by default with all of Microsoft Research. In this monorepo for example was the proven-capable edge scale pretraining codebase I talked about in the COLM keynote last month. This might seem like a minor detail, but the amount effort required to create a well-formed model creation pipeline is substantial and I’m aware of at least 4 efforts (the other 3 not in public-within-MSR repos) trying to develop model building pipelines.
In early September we were reorged into Microsoft AI. On the surface this could make sense, because putting two different AI organizations together creates opportunities for better concentration of effort, and there were places where AIF was ahead of MAI and of course vice-versa (MAI is much larger). In practice, there are substantial issues because the philosophy of the ex-Inflection leadership of MAI is incompatible. The core philosophy there is scaling, and aggressively not research. This might shock some folks who naturally think that the way you make better models is via research but there is plenty of evidence that bigger models are better models as far as the quality of the predictions they make and from a business perspective returns to scale are far more predictable than returns to research. Cult.fit is one of India’s leading technology-enabled fitness companies, operating 708 fitness centers across 77 cities and serving nearly one million paid members. Its business combines subscription-based access to gyms and trainer-led fitness classes with a growing consumer products portfolio spanning fitness equipment, accessories, workout footwear and activewear.
As the company grew, it wanted to solve more operational and product challenges without adding layers of process and complexity. By standardizing engineering on Codex and then extending it beyond engineering, cult.fit is helping teams across the organization analyze data, build tools, and move ideas into production. Alongside its Codex rollout, it is using the OpenAI API to develop more personalized member experiences, including through its AI Trainer.
For Santhosh Kumar, CTO at cult.fit, AI presented an opportunity to change how the organization works. “We wanted to become more AI-native in the way we run things,” he says. “How can we run our operations or transform our operations to be AI-first? What new customer experiences can we offer? And how can we transform how we run our organization?”
Cult.fit’s first major shift was in engineering. Before standardizing on Codex, developers were using a mix of coding agents and assistants. Different tools meant different conventions for repositories, agent instructions, skills, and development workflows, making it harder to share knowledge and reuse capabilities across teams.
Cult.fit wanted a shared platform around which it could standardize the software development lifecycle. The company chose Codex as that foundation. Repository structures, skills, testing, code review, and feedback loops could now follow common conventions across teams.
“Once we standardized on Codex, we could build our software development lifecycle around a single platform.”

Its Site Reliability Engineering agent can aggregate information from observability platforms and logs, investigate incidents, and, in many cases, create a pull request with a proposed fix for an engineer to review. Cult.fit is also moving toward a more fully spec-driven development model, where a specification can guide work through the software development lifecycle toward a pull request for an engineer to review. This gives teams a more repeatable path from a defined requirement to working code.

Fast and cost-effective at scale
Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.
Longer clips up to 15 seconds
You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.

You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.

news.title: Underdog shows off a 32MB speech model in new demo
news.summary_raw: Despite its small size, Underdog's new model can generate both speech and music.
news.source_text:
AI companies across the world are racing to make bigger and better models, but the problem is all of them need massive amounts of processing power. On the other end, some researchers and startups are creating smaller models that can run on edge devices, like your phone or computer.
One such startup, Underdog, has released a game built with its new voice model called Woof that’s only 32MB large.
The game features a room with a retro tech theme, a typewriter, and a CRT monitor. There is a desk lamp, which makes a sound when you click its switch. The intro warns users about “intrusive” cloud providers in the town — ostensibly a jab at cloud-based models.
You can interact with the typewriter and music tuner.
You can type anything on the typewriter using your keyboard, and the game will speak it back. You can also rotate the tuner to generate different kinds of music.
All of this works within the browser through Underdog’s speech generation model, which, the company says, can run on most devices without any internet connection. The model has 31 million parameters and is open for everyone to download.
While such a small model likely won’t replace bigger models, it may still be enough to drive local assistant experiences or create personalized podcasts.
This demo comes weeks after Underdog launched Bark, a 167 MB speech-to-text model also designed to run on edge devices for transcription and dictation.
Sigil Wen, the founder of Underdog, told TechCrunch that he started building the app because, instead of using notetakers like Granola, he wanted to build his own system with AI models that can run on users’ devices and let them own their data.
“I think we will be able to run most capable models of today on the devices you already own within months. We just want to train the best open models that are American-made, that are open, that are capable and allow people to have private AI,” he said, referring to his manifesto.
In addition to the two voice models mentioned above, Underdog has also released a 27-billion-parameter model that can run on laptops, along with a waitlisted app that the company is positioning as a locally-hosted alternative to Muse and Instinct.
news.summary: Underdog has released a 32 MB voice model called Woof that runs entirely on local devices, enabling offline speech generation in browsers without cloud dependency. The model, open‑source and designed for edge deployment, could support lightweight assistant or personalization workloads on end‑user machines.

news.title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
news.source_text:
ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation
Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.
To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.
Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.
Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.
ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.
Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.
How ToyBlocks works
Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.
As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.
Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.
Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.
A physical robot gripper
news.summary: Hugging Face has released ToyBlocks, a controlled simulation framework that lets researchers automatically generate tasks and training demonstrations for robot arm manipulation. The platform emphasizes repeatable experiments, realistic physics, and scalability for studying learning dynamics.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on ToyBlocks for future integration opportunities if your organization explores robotic automation or AI-driven process optimization. Evaluate whether the framework could be adapted to simulate internal workflow scenarios or test new automation scripts before deployment.
