news.title: Meta quietly launches an AI fashion app called Style Sketch
news.summary_raw: The app connects to Instagram to build a virtual closet from photos you’ve already shared, or lets you add items manually by snapping a photo, recording a quick video, or uploading images from your camera roll.
news.source_text:
Meta has quietly launched Style Sketch, an AI fashion app that helps users put together outfit ideas using clothes they already own. The app connects to Instagram to build a virtual closet from photos you’ve posted, or lets you add items manually by snapping a photo, recording a quick video, or uploading images from your camera roll.
Style Sketch then suggests outfit combinations built from your wardrobe matched to your style. Users can then try on the outfits on a “realistic model matched to your body shape and skin tone,” the app description reads.
The app, which was first spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra, is available in Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand on iOS and Android.
Meta did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment. It’s unknown whether Meta plans to launch Style Sketch more widely.
Several apps already use AI to help users digitize their wardrobes and visualize new outfits, including startups like Alta. Even Google Photos offers tools that let users turn photos of their clothes into digital closets where they can create new outfit ideas.
To compete with what’s already on the market, Meta will likely rely less on the novelty of the idea and more on the app’s integration with Instagram, where users already have a visual record of their personal style.
Rather than relying on random suggestions, users can also select a specific item from their wardrobe and get fresh outfit ideas built around it, according to the app description.
The app can also help users plan outfits for trips. If they enter their destination, trip length, and planned activities, users can get a day-by-day outfit plan that takes the weather forecast and itinerary into account.
Style Sketch is one of many AI apps from Meta in recent months. Most recently, the company launched an app called Waddle World, which essentially looks like a Tamagotchi clone, but with AI. Meta has also launched Pocket, a tool for vibe-coding games, and Vibes, which lets users quickly generate AI-powered videos.
The wave of new apps is part of a broader effort at Meta to release more apps. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this year that CEO Mark Zuckerberg told employees the company plans to release far more apps than it has historically, as AI-driven efficiencies have made it faster and easier to ship new apps.
news.summary: Meta has quietly released Style Sketch, an AI-powered fashion app that builds a virtual closet from Instagram photos and suggests outfits based on user wardrobe. The app, available in Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand on iOS and Android, offers AI-generated outfit combos and trip planning features.
news.enterprise_use: Check your team’s user data policies for any Instagram integration and assess whether you need to update privacy settings or data handling procedures. Missing this review could expose your organization to unintended data sharing with Meta’s app ecosystem.

news.summary_raw:

news.source_text:
We're reaching out to inform you of a security incident involving one of our infrastructure providers, the steps we've taken, and what this means for you.
- What happened and how we responded
Last week, one of our infrastructure providers reported unauthorized access involving third-party server management software. One of our CDN nodes, located in Armenia, was hosted on a server supplied by this provider.
After receiving the alert from the affected provider, our engineering team took immediate action. Within 20 minutes, we stopped routing traffic through the server. We then reviewed and preserved the relevant security logs for investigation, securely wiped the server, and revoked its access to our other systems. The affected server has been permanently removed from our infrastructure.
Our investigation found no evidence of unauthorized access to the CDN node or any of its data. The infrastructure provider has also found no evidence that our server was accessed, but continues to investigate the incident.
- What this means for your data
While neither investigation has found any indication of unauthorized access to our server, we cannot completely rule out the possibility.
If unauthorized access to our CDN node did occur, the potentially exposed information would have been: temporarily cached CDN content, Pull Zone configurations, and TLS certificates stored on that server.
As an additional precaution, we have revoked and reissued all TLS certificates for bunny.net platform domains (b-cdn.net and bunny.run). Reissuance of managed TLS certificates for custom domains is ongoing and is expected to be completed within the next 24 hours. No action is required from customers using managed certificates. We will post a further update on our status page once this process is complete.
If you manage your own TLS certificates, we recommend revoking and reissuing them with new private keys as a precaution.
No other customer data, including bunny.net account data, was stored on the server in question, and no internal systems were affected.
- What happens next
We’re closely monitoring our infrastructure and working with the affected provider as the investigation continues. Should any new findings affect our customers, we will provide an update via email and on our status page.
At bunny.net, we understand the trust you place in us to keep your content secure, and we take that responsibility seriously. If you have any questions or need help with managing your TLS certificates, our support team will be happy to assist.
            
            
              Posted Oct 28, 2026 - 11:40 UTC
news.summary: Bunny CDN experienced a security incident where an unauthorized access event was detected in a server supplied by an infrastructure provider. The incident prompted an immediate shutdown, data review, and TLS certificate reissuance, with no confirmed data breach.
news.enterprise_use: S1: Inspect your own TLS certificates and revoke/reissue any that are managed through Bunny CDN or similar third‑party CDN services this week. S2: Failing to do so could expose temporary cached content, Pull Zone configurations, or TLS keys if an attacker gained access. S3: The most affected area for your IT stack is your CDN and any custom domain certificate management, which may intersect with your existing certificate lifecycle tools.

news.title: Intel’s stock crashes, knocking $12B from government’s stake
news.summary_raw: Intel is being hurt by PC sales as the AI industry gobbles memory and other components causing PC prices to rise.
news.source_text:
Intel’s stock suffered one of its worst days ever on Friday, crashing around 28% after the chip giant reported a weaker-than-expected outlook for the fourth quarter.
This route reduced the value of Intel’s holdings by the government by $12 billion, CNBC reports. The Trump administration had the government buy 10% stake over a year ago. Nvidia, which also took a big stake in Intel in 2025, saw its stock drop a bit on Friday as well. Much of the tech industry — especially chipmakers — were caught in the selloff.
Intel’s stock is still a profitable investment for the government so far (and for Nvidia), as it’s up more than 70% for the year, even if its dropped significantly from the sky high prices it commanded over the summer.
The scare-off was caused when Intel warned to expect revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion in the fourth quarter when analysts were looking for around $17 billion. It also warned that its gross profit margin would decline to 37% from the 43%, and it was investing so heavily, it expected no positive cash flow.
The main problem for Intel is that PC sales are being hurt by the AI industry gobbling memory and other components, and causing PC prices to rise.
“Our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on the memory prices and availability. Year-to-date system endpoint prices have increased significantly, placing additional pressure on already limited IT budgets,” Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan warned on the call.
The bright side is that revenue from Intel’s data center business grew 78% over the year-ago quarter. But it is hamstrung on that front until it can bring more capacity to its fabs and book more external customers for them, competing with powerhouse Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. One of Intel’s new fabs in Arizona is operational but the next one isn’t expected to be online until 2028.
news.summary: Intel’s shares plunged 28% after the company cut its Q4 revenue and margin forecasts, wiping $12 billion off the U.S. government’s stake in the chipmaker. The sell‑off rattles the broader semiconductor market, potentially tightening budgets for hardware procurement in IT operations.
news.enterprise_use: Watch Intel’s pricing and supply‑chain announcements for the next 30 days, as higher memory and processor costs could raise the total cost of ownership for endpoint devices and data‑center infrastructure in your organization.

news.title: Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences
news.summary_raw: OpenAI will honor a shared robots.txt signal to help website operators communicate their AI training preferences to participating providers.
news.source_text:
Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences
Why we’re supporting a common signal that lets website operators communicate their choices to multiple AI providers at once.
Today, we’re announcing that OpenAI will honor a common signal(opens in a new window) in robots.txt, the file that lets websites express their preferences about the use of their content for foundational generative AI training. This voluntary effort makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.
Previously, website operators would identify individual crawlers and maintain separate rules for each and every provider. Having a shared signal across multiple providers reduces that work for operators.
We aim to implement the signal in the coming months, and will share another update with details about our implementation when we do so. This new signal will not replace the controls we already provide through robots.txt. Our existing crawler controls(opens in a new window), which provide web publishers flexibility and control over their pages, will continue to apply and be respected.
This draws on the ongoing work(opens in a new window) of the Internet Engineering Task Force’s (IETF) AI Preferences working group. We’re joining other participants in the working group in today’s announcement of this shared signal, and believe this strengthens our continued participation in the IETF standards discussions. OpenAI will continue to adapt its practices as those conversations and the landscape continue to evolve in view of appropriate controls and fairness.
We believe this is a practical step toward an open web where people can publish and discover information, and website owners have clearer, simpler ways to communicate their choices about how their content is used. We encourage other AI providers to honor the signal.
news.summary: OpenAI will honor a new shared signal in robots.txt that lets website operators communicate AI training preferences to multiple AI providers at once. The change simplifies content usage control for publishers but does not directly alter the IT tools the engineer manages.
news.enterprise_use: Monitor the upcoming implementation updates from OpenAI; if your organization hosts websites or relies on web content for internal tools, keep an eye on the new robots.txt signal so you can update your web content management policies accordingly. This will help ensure compliance with evolving AI data usage norms and avoid unintended data exposure.

news.title: Fair use benefits everyone
news.summary_raw: OpenAI shares excerpts from court briefs by creators, academics, accessibility advocates, and legal experts, among others, on how fair use supports AI training and innovation.
news.source_text:
Fair use benefits everyone
Authors, journalists, creators, academics, accessibility advocates, legal experts, librarians, economists and business leaders are voicing their support for the longstanding principle of fair use and its application to AI training.
For decades, fair use has played a critical role in driving innovation that benefits everyone. It has helped deliver important medical and scientific breakthroughs and new technologies that have made real and positive differences for countless people, including authors and journalists. The New York Times’ lawsuit, meanwhile, asks everyone to ignore a half century of legal history and progress, and toss aside the longstanding principle of fair use in their own narrow pursuit of an undeserved payday.
Experts and leaders across a wide range of fields have recognized that fair use is a win-win that benefits everyone, and have shared their perspectives with the Court in filing briefs in support of fair use.
Below you’ll find excerpts from some of those submissions, in their own words. The full filings are available on the public court docket, and you can read more about fair use and AI here.
AI Progress
The Court should reject Plaintiffs’ attempt to extend copyright beyond its established limits. AI training uses copyrighted works for a fundamentally different purpose, does not provide the public with substitute access to those works, and does not cause the market harm cognizable under the Copyright Act. Instead, it enables a broad array of transformative technologies that are already delivering public benefits. Copyright exists to promote creativity and progress, not to suppress lawful innovation or protect authors from competition. Settled fair use principles therefore compel the conclusion that generative AI training is fair use.
American Council of the Blind, Association of Research Libraries, American Library Association, Consumer Technology Association & Business Software Alliance
This case concerns more than companies that develop large language models (LLMs). It affects medical researchers and patients, educators serving students with different learning needs, people with disabilities seeking greater independence, farmers applying agricultural knowledge, independent creators developing new forms of expression, and industry sectors from software to the law. news.title: Anthropic expected to receive high ‘junk’ rating from credit agencies following IPO, report says
news.summary_raw: The new report says the AI lab will likely qualify for a high junk rating.
news.source_text:
Anthropic is expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit rating agencies following its initial public offering, according to a report from the Financial Times.
The FT says the investment giant Blackstone, the investment giant and anchor investor in a recent $63 billion deal to finance Anthropic’s chips, told investors in the deal that it expects the AI lab to receive a “high” junk rating after its IPO. Previously, the FT notes, Blackstone had said the opposite: that the Claude-maker would receive an investment-grade rating (indicating low risk for lenders) before 2027 rolls around.
Now, Blackstone expects double B range rating, the top tier of speculative “junk” grade, according to the reporting.
TechCrunch reached out to Anthropic and Blackstone but both declined to comment.
Blackstone’s forecast is just a prediction, but naturally, a high junk rating would make it more difficult and costlier for Anthropic to raise the money to keep funding its massive spending that has undergirded its business. The lab has been on a spending spree, wracking up large compute power deals throughout the past 12 months, which has worried investors.
Anthropic officially filed to go public earlier this week, kicking off a wave of speculation about how the massive IPO would impact the broader AI industry.
news.summary: Anthropic’s IPO filing has prompted a forecast of a high junk credit rating from Blackstone, potentially increasing borrowing costs for the AI lab.

Building a Haunted House with NVIDIA Nemotron Open Models
Or rather…
Boo! Now Get Off My Lawn!
TL;DR: MonsterHouse is an interactive projection I created for Halloween. He listens to trick-or-treaters, answers in the voice of a grumpy old pirate ship and softens when visitors remember their manners. He is built on the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent with NVIDIA Nemotron ASR, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, Magpie TTS Zeroshot and Audio2Face-3D, and he runs on a single workstation.
I wanted the kids visiting my house at Halloween to interact in a fun and unique way. The house was going to be in charge and giving out the treats, but more grumpy than scary. Somehow, my solution was to give the garage door a mouth and teach him to complain.
That became MonsterHouse: a grumpy old building with pirate stories, a fiery grin and a suspicious weakness for “please.” NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent supplies the conversation foundation. Nemotron Speech does the listening, Bolt E4B is the brain, NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot is the live voice, and NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D makes the wooden mouth talk.
How Monster House works
- Listening: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 ASR turns visitor speech into text. [
nemotron-speech-streaming-en-0.6b.q8_0.gguf]- Thinking: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open small language model for conversational agents, writes each reply. A LoRA adapter supplies the personality.
- Speaking: NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot voices each reply from a short reference sample of the character.
- Animating: NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D turns clean speech into mouth animation in Unreal Engine 5.
- Seeing: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni describes costumes, while YOLO and ByteTrack count and track visitors.
- Running it: NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent coordinates everything on one workstation with an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q and an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell.
A grin full of splinters
The mouth came first. I imagined the wooden garage door boards splitting into jagged lips, with the burning flames of hell illuminating the driveway from beyond whenever he opened his cursed mouth. He needed to look ancient, expressive and mildly offended by the existence of visitors.
A few expressions from a house with plenty to say.
Creating a custom animation rig was one of the more labor intensive parts of the build. After bashing it into submission, I could export the facial expression shapes that Audio2Face-3D could later animate. The character SkelMesh was built in Autodesk Maya then exported into Unreal Engine where virtual fire and effects were added behind the door. With no eyes, no eyebrows and no blinking, he’s a surprisingly economical monster.
While all the nonsense of building the character was going on, NVIDIA built the Nemotron Voice Agent. What was supposed to be the hard part of the build now became rather fun, iterative and easy. I had a foundation for listening, conversation and speech right out of the box. The house already had a mouth. Now he could finally fi

news.title: Last-minute Halloween costumes for tech nerds
news.summary_raw: No Halloween costume? Just be a deceptively cute AI agent icon, a PHP vulnerability, or sleepy time Bryan Johnson.

It happens to the best of us — you’ve completely dropped the ball on figuring out a Halloween costume. Naturally, you’ve decided to solve this problem by turning to… TechCrunch? Yeah, sure, why not. I’ve got some ideas.

Recursive self-improvement

I’m not sure how to visually represent the idea of an AI building itself, but you could really lean into the “self-improvement” part and forget the “recursive” aspect — it’s a last-minute Halloween costume. You don’t need to try that hard.
Dress as the version of yourself you imagine becoming every year when you make New Year’s resolutions. Leave in the middle of the party to “go to therapy” when you actually just want to go home. Brag to people about how good your Oura Ring’s sleep score is.
You are the embodiment of someone trying to better themselves. You are recursive self-improvement.
A deceptively cute AI agent
Meta and OpenAI both recently launched AI assistants with creepily cute avatars. It’s almost Elizabeth Holmes-esque — they look innocent, so you underestimate their potential to cause disaster. (While we’re talking about her, you’re only allowed to do the black turtleneck Holmes costume if you’re a natural blonde, or if you have a blonde wig.)
What you’re going to do is make yourself look big and fluffy. Maybe you have a poofy puffer jacket, or maybe you can find some colorful feather boas to wrap yourself in. Throughout the night, ask people if you can obtain read/write access to their Gmail.

news.title: Zero click, silent, remote Android DoS
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://smsofdeath.com/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50285452
Points: 151
# Comments: 97
news.source_text:
Android Telephony · Zero-Click · Remote DoS
A single malformed WAP Push SMS crashes com.android.phone on Android, dropping active calls (including emergency calls), with zero interaction from the victim.
⚠ Working proof-of-concept, authorised testing only. Read the warning & license before downloading.
When Android receives a WAP Push message, WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu() reads the WSP header length as a uintvar. The value comes back as a long, is cast to int with no range check, and is then used directly as the size of a new byte array:
// WapPushOverSms.java:217  header length read as long, cast with no bounds check
int headerLength = (int) pduDecoder.getValue32();
    ...
// WapPushOverSms.java:244  the cast value is used as an array size
byte[] header = new byte[headerLength];A 5-byte uintvar of 88 80 80 80 00 decodes to 0x80000000. Cast to a signed 32-bit int, that is -2147483648. Allocating new byte[-2147483648] throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException on the telephony main thread, killing com.android.phone:
E AndroidRuntime: FATAL EXCEPTION: main
E AndroidRuntime: Process: com.android.phone
E AndroidRuntime: java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException: -2147483648
E AndroidRuntime:   at ...WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:244)
E AndroidRuntime:   at ...WapPushOverSms.dispatchWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:339)
E AndroidRuntime:   at ...InboundSmsHandler.processMessagePart(InboundSmsHandler.java:1169)
E AndroidRuntime:   at ...InboundSmsHandler$DeliveringState.processMessage(InboundSmsHandler.java:627)The message is delivered as a data SMS and is never shown to the user: there is nothing in the inbox, and the victim never sees the sender's number.
DisconnectCause CS_DEATH as the process restarts.com.android.phone restarts.Tested across multiple makes and models (Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware, various Samsung Galaxy and A-series) with a 100% reproduction rate.
A single message is a repeated transient outage. Sending the payload rapidly in succession (≈30 messages) is materially worse: the crashes interleave with the telephony provider's writes to the SMS store and hit a race condition that corrupts the SQLite database holding the device's messages.
Once the database is corrupt, com.android.phone no longer needs a fresh message to fail: it crashes immediately on every boot as it reads the damaged store. The phone is now persistently without telephony, and a restart does not clear it.
Recovery is hostile, and this is the critical part: a factory reset only helps temporarily, because the carrier re-sends the unacknowledged payload and re-triggers the crash. Full recovery required:
On a device using an eSIM, where the SIM can't simply be moved to another handset, recovery would be significantly harder, and for a non-technical user, effectively out of reach.
This is the distinction the report turns on. It is not a transient crash: it is a remote, zero-click, persistent denial of service requiring a factory reset (and more) to recover,
news.summary: Android’s telephony stack has a zero‑click, silent DoS flaw that crashes the phone’s call handler via a malformed WAP Push SMS, causing persistent loss of telephony including emergency calls. The flaw requires a factory reset and can be triggered without user interaction, making it a severe risk for mobile device users.
news.enterprise_use: S1: Immediately audit all Android devices managed through your MDM platform for firmware versions vulnerable to this exploit and apply the latest security patches or roll out a hotfix. S2: Failure to patch exposes employees to persistent phone outages, potentially disrupting business communications and exposing them to legal liabilities if emergency services are unreachable. S3: This issue most directly impacts the mobile endpoint security component of your stack, so prioritize it in your device management and incident response playbooks.

news.title: Forging a Microsoft Edge Full Chain with Logic Bugs Only
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://blog.orange.tw/posts/2026-10-the-last-proof-of-human-craft-browser-full-chain/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50285319

news.source_text:
I think I should still dump some of my work once in a while, even though it feels like fewer and fewer people actually sit down and read articles these days (or maybe now they all leave it to their agents XD). Anyway, this is what I built for Pwn2Own Berlin 2026 — a completely handmade, logic-only Microsoft Edge Full Chain, with no memory corruption, and no AI at all! 🔥
Confirmed! Orange Tsai (@orange_8361) of DEVCORE Research Team (@d3vc0r3) chained 4 logic bugs to achieve a sandbox escape on Microsoft Edge, earning $175,000 and 17.5 Master of Pwn points. Full win! #Pwn2Own #P2OBerlin https://t.co/vJaIpGG4cD
— TrendAI Zero Day Initiative (@thezdi) May 14, 2026
The whole chain is made up of five bugs and two Windows features. I have also shared the whole bug-hunting and chaining process at this year’s HITCON and Hexacon, plus some fun stories along the way. You can check the slides here!
Also, maybe everyone thinks LLMs can already pwn everything in the AI era, so something made entirely by hand somehow feels a bit more precious. That might also be why this chain was nominated for this year’s Pwnie Awards and won the Epic Achievement award. 🎉
Let’s Navigate!
So where do we start with a logic-only full chain? Well, since it’s a “browser,” let’s start by looking at how “browsing” (or what Chromium calls “navigation”) works. I won’t go into too much detail in this post, because I think in this era, you can just ask your agents to fill in the details :)
But I’d still recommend reading “Life of a Navigation“ from Chrome University if you want to get the full picture.
The Forgotten Navigation Throttles
While I was walking through the Chromium Navigation flow, something called “Navigation Throttles” caught my attention. They live in the Browser Process, and intercept all navigation requests initiated by either the Browser or the Renderer. Maybe it’s easy to say this in hindsight, but out of the 3,000+ CVEs Google Chrome has fixed over the past five years, there are only fewer than 20 related to them. So I guess this is also a corner not too many people pay attention to.
Anyway, I started digging into the Navigation Throttles, and checked how Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge implemented them. And while going through the code, I found that Edge has a throttle called EdgeCAGuidanceNavigationThrottle for its enterprise Entra ID feature (the CA here stands for Conditional Access). The purpose of this throttle is to guide users to the right User Profile when Edge detects them signing in with a work account on a Microsoft website. And to fire this throttle, you have to start a navigation from a specific Microsoft-owned origin, such as login.live.com:
And once the throttle is fired, Edge would compare the email of the current User Profile with ?email={email}. If they don’t match, Edge pops up a dialog guiding you to switch accounts.
But if they do match, Edge would then grab the URL you were originally heading to from switch_profile={url}, and launch a new navi
news.summary: Security researchers chained five logic bugs in Microsoft Edge, bypassing memory corruption to escape the sandbox. The exploit targets Edge’s Conditional Access Navigation Throttle used with Entra ID, exposing enterprise users to credential misuse.

news.title: Microsoft hits 10 quarters of record-breaking revenue in a row
news.summary_raw: Whatever the future of AI might be, the current situation is still very good for Microsoft. The tech giant reported yet another record for quarterly revenue on Wednesday: $92.3 billion, a 19% increase over the year-ago quarter.
news.source_text:
Whatever the future of AI might be, the current situation is still very good for Microsoft. The tech giant reported yet another quarterly revenue record on Wednesday: $92.3 billion, a 19% increase over the year-ago quarter.
Microsoft has now reported record-breaking revenue for 10 quarters in a row.
This is profitable revenue, too. Microsoft reported that net income reached $36.6 billion, an increase of 32% on a GAAP basis, over the year-ago quarter.
The record-breaking income was largely driven on the strength of Microsoft Cloud, which reached $63.9 billion in revenue this quarter, an increase of 30% over the year-ago quarter, Microsoft said.
Microsoft has reorganized its business reporting into two basic segments: 1) Agents and Infra and 2) Devices and Consumer. On the flip side, revenue in Devices and Consumer was $15.5 billion, decreased of 3%, with Windows OEM and devices revenue falling 22% from the year-ago quarter.
True, not all of Microsoft’s healthy cloud revenue can be attributed to AI. Microsoft 365 accounted for nearly $28 billion. But Azure brought in the most, at $33.2 billion. And again, not all of that is necessarily AI-related. Enterprises run all sorts of the traditional software and SaaS applications on Azure.
Still, a good chunk of the revenue was from AI, because Microsoft also reported $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI. Despite branching out to AWS, Oracle, and others, OpenAI still runs a lot of its services on Microsoft’s cloud. (Anthropic runs on Azure as well.) Microsoft also said its “commercial remaining performance obligation increased 73% to $677 billion.” That represents future revenue committed under existing contracts of the AI labs.
But, like all the big cloud providers, Microsoft is also spending big to prepare to deliver on those commitments. Capital expenditures topped $45.2 billion, another all-time quarterly record.
news.summary: Microsoft reported a record-breaking 10th consecutive quarter of revenue, driven largely by its cloud and AI businesses, including a $10 billion hit from OpenAI services on Azure. The revenue surge underscores the growing commercial weight of AI within Microsoft’s core enterprise stack, directly impacting Azure, Microsoft 365, and related licensing models.

news.title: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms
news.source_text:
Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms
Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.
Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.
In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.
Today we're announcing two packages:
- AnySpeechRecognizer implements Apple's new speech-to-text API with a choice of recognition engine, including NVIDIA's Parakeet and Alibaba's Qwen3-ASR running locally on Core ML, and adds speaker diarization to track who speaks when.
- AnyDecisionModel answers yes-or-no, multiple-choice, and rating-scale questions with typed results and probabilities. It derives each answer from the model's probabilities instead of generating text, using a model on your device with MLX, Core AI, or llama.cpp, or a decision model from Jev or Ollama.
Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.
AnySpeechRecognizer
Computers have been transcribing speech for decades,
and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it.
Apple platforms already have an API for it.
macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer,
Apple's new speech-to-text API.
You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer,
give it a file or a stream of audio buffers,
and read results from async sequences as they arrive.
AssetInventory installs the models,
so your app decides when downloads happen.
It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:
- import Speech
+ import AnySpeechRecognizer
The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber,
SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory,
with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine.
If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough.
To use Parakeet instead,
change only how you create the transcriber:
let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(
    model: ParakeetSpeechModel(variant: .v3),
    transcriptionOptions: [],
    reportingOptions: [.volatileResults],
    attributeOptions: [.audioTimeRange]
)
The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.
Meet the models
Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a lo
news.summary: Hugging Face has released two Swift packages, AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel, enabling Apple developers to swap out Apple's native speech-to-text engine for alternatives like NVIDIA’s Parakeet and Alibaba’s Qwen3-ASR, and to run decision models locally on device. These open models can be downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub and run on Core ML, MLX, Core AI or llama.cpp, offering faster, cheaper, and more flexible AI processing for iOS and macOS apps.

news.title: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth
news.summary_raw: Critical flaw in EDK2 allows attackers to execute code early in the boot process.
news.source_text:
Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.
The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.
The cat has left the bag
The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes-Mitra of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.
With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.
news.summary: A critical code‑execution vulnerability (CVE‑2026‑97631) was discovered in the TianoCore EDK II UEFI firmware used by most server vendors and cloud providers. The flaw can allow pre‑OS malicious code execution, bypassing Secure Boot protections, and requires immediate patching of affected firmware builds.
news.enterprise_use: S1: Inspect the firmware versions on your infrastructure and verify if they incorporate the latest EDK II updates or Microsoft Project Mu patches; apply the official fixes this week. S2: Failure to patch could expose your servers to boot‑time attacks that evade standard OS‑level defenses, potentially compromising cloud workloads and on‑prem services. S3: This directly impacts the security posture of any cloud hosts you manage through Azure, AWS, or on‑prem data centers, so prioritize firmware audit in your JumpCloud and Freshservice ticketing.

news.title: Anthropic just launched tools to show companies what their AI spending is buying
news.summary_raw: The frontier lab is lifting the curtain on how users spend money on its models ahead of a planned IPO.
news.source_text:
The financials Anthropic shared with investors this week suggest that its AI coding tool, Claude Code, is every bit the business success the frontier lab wanted. The company recorded an operating profit in the second quarter, and 900% net revenue retention — that is, spending from the same customers in Q3 2025 grew nine times in Q3 2026.
Anthropic has focused on getting enterprise users to stick around and Wednesday announced a new suite of reporting tools designed to give those customers a more granular understanding of the value they get from their token spend.
Using internal analytics and employee surveys, managers can view a team’s work over a given date range, what the team produced, how much it cost, and where its workflows broke down. Anthropic says it won’t use this data for model training by default. The reports will also offer recommendations on how to improve the results.
This is a clear attempt to demonstrate the return on investment of Anthropic’s tools and to show customers how to improve it — a major concern among large customers. Anthropic is also creating pooled group budgets to allow teams to better manage token spending.
Businesses have been hunting for that kind of information as they figure out how best to deploy AI tools. While usage among venture-backed firms is driving token spend, most of the Fortune 500 are not seeing major gains from deploying AI.
Jellyfish, a company that makes tools for software developers, released a new report yesterday based on the use of agentic coding tools by 276,000 of its customers. Claude Code and other tools built on Anthropic models remain the most widely used in the survey, responsible for nearly a third of all proposed code changes submitted for review. More importantly, spending on those tools has grown 10x since the beginning of the year, with their cost now equal to about 2% of total engineering cost.
“Even if you’re saying 2% is still small, that 10x growth is growth that most CFOs didn’t plan for,” Nicholas Arcolano, the chief scientist at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. We’re certainly getting to the point where people are realizing, okay, it’s not enough to just spend a bunch. You now have to optimize it, make it work.”
Anthropic’s new reports speak to that challenge. Anthropic leads among enterprise customers, but what makes an agentic coding tool truly sticky is difficult to identify. The release of OpenAI’s Astra model this summer seemed like a potential threat to Anthropic, but so far it hasn’t slowed Anthropic’s adoption numbers.

Looking at X, he continued, you’d get the distinct impression that the competition is more heated. “Everyone in the Valley is like, ‘Oh, Codex is better.’” In reality, Albarran continued, “Anthropic was just there with great enterprise motions, and they had an i
news.summary: Anthropic has unveiled a new suite of reporting tools that let enterprise customers track token spend, output quality, and cost breakdowns for their AI coding tool, Claude Code. These dashboards aim to help organizations optimize AI ROI and manage budgets without the data feeding back into model training.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on Anthropic’s reporting feature as a potential cost‑tracking tool for your own AI deployments. If your team uses Claude Code or similar services, evaluate how these metrics could inform your internal budgeting and approval processes. This may reduce over‑spending and improve justification for future AI spend.

news.title: I Put a Bunch of AI Agents in Charge of a Fantasy Soccer Team. They’re Not Better Than Humans—Yet
news.summary_raw: To experiment with AI’s predictive skills, I let Codex loose on a fantasy team. It tried to bench Erling Haaland at first, but it soon learned the error of its ways.
news.source_text:
I have consulted my AI-powered crystal ball, and it’s telling me that frontier models are going to get a lot better at making predictions in the near future. Just ask my Premier League fantasy team.
A few weeks ago, I deployed a small horde of AI agents to craft and manage an experimental roster. Given the proliferation of AI agents into pretty much every aspect of our lives, I wanted to know if a swarm of bots could put together a winning team.
I first looked at the potential for AI here a few years ago, playing around with a tool from the UK’s Turing Institute that selected teams after modeling previous fantasy league data. Its suggestions were remarkably bonkers—it didn’t incorporate real-world information, like a player’s injury or a team’s change in management.
This time, while on a flight to visit family, I asked Codex for help. First, I fed the model a couple of relevant research papers. Then, I asked it to build a harness—instructions and code that guides different agents through various steps—that would check recent news and run a model to make predictions.
It quickly came up with a setup that seemed to collate and analyze way more information than I ever would have. And yet I was surprised by how dumb the initial team suggestions were. Leaving Erling Haaland on the bench? Really, Codex?
I then asked Codex to create a team of agents that did different things: several that read news and blog posts; others that analyzed recent results; more that ran models; and a bunch that critiqued suggestions. This seemed to significantly improve the suggestions. I tried increasing the number of agents to more than 100, hoping this would make the system smarter still, but it didn’t change much besides running up my API bill.
Still, the improvement from a few years ago was striking. According to Haifeng Xu, a computer scientist at the University of Chicago who studies the uses of AI in market situations, newer models may be even better at making predictions because they’re able to consume and analyze huge amounts of real-world information, and they’re able to orchestrate more complex systems for their guesses.
“AI is just getting smarter in understanding the world—I feel like that's the fundamental reason they’re improving,” Xu tells me.
Late last year, Xu was marveling at the growing popularity of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket. He wondered how the best commercial models might fare on those markets, so alongside several colleagues, he began testing their forecasting skills.
They had models guess, for example, who would win the NBA Championship and who President Trump would meet with.
“Very quickly we started to realize that models did really well,” Xu tells me. The models were sometimes able to do better than the average person without any special instructions or guidance, he says. In their testing, GPT-5 was the best at making predictions, followed by Grok 4, Claude Sonnet, Gemini, and Llama.

news.summary: Wired AI reports an experiment where AI agents were deployed to manage a fantasy soccer team, showcasing the limits of current models like Codex and GPT‑5 in complex, real‑world decision making. The study illustrates that, despite advances, AI still struggles with nuanced, up‑to‑date data integration and cost efficiency.

news.title: I Gave My Blood to the AI Death Clock
news.summary_raw: Death Clock promises to predict when you’re going to die and help you extend your time on Earth. After a month, I felt like it was sucking the life out of me.
news.source_text:
I am scheduled to die on August 10, 2060, at the age of 74.
So says my iPhone screen, where Death Clock, an AI-powered longevity app that predicts life expectancy based on your medical habits and lifestyle, has produced an image of a smiling grim reaper to celebrate my expiration date. There he was one September morning, looking especially thrilled about the reveal, gesturing with a peace sign as he reclined in a doughnut-shaped pool inflatable under that giant number: 74.
I have never resented getting older, but I suppose that’s younger than I’d like to be when my time is up. In the last four years—years that brought the passing of my grandmother and aunt within 18 months—I’ve become hyperaware of how finite my days are. Since turning 40 in January, I’ve also experienced daily reminders of aging: inexplicable pains that rotate between my back, neck, and hips. Spiritually, I feel young; physically, my body screams otherwise. Aging is natural, but I had a creeping suspicion I could buy myself more time.
Our collective obsession with life extension has given rise to a multitrillion-dollar longevity industry, bolstered by wannabe prophets like Bryan Johnson. Threats like climate change and AI doomerism only seem to have intensified existential fears, even as LLMs promise a new era of personalized medicine to address any health issue. Track enough pieces of data, the thinking goes, and algorithms can help you hack your own demise.
All of which led me to Death Clock, an app launched in 2024 aimed at tracking users’ health habits in an attempt to prolong their lives. In February, the company announced a new feature that lets you order biomarker panels. For a $69 subscription, you can get a basic blood panel that measures things like cholesterol, blood sugars, inflammation, vitamin D, and blood and organ health. There are also nine additional tests—assessing everything from hormones and micronutrients to your thyroid—that, altogether, cost $780. I opted for the routine blood panel and added the “stress” test ($29). Maybe some new insight could help me get a handle on it.
In an attempt to be more than another morbid countdown gimmick, Death Clock says it’s trained its AI on 1,200 longevity studies, actuarial data from life insurance companies, and life expectancy tables. Based on your results, its algorithms create a detailed prevention plan intended to help extend the time you have left.
Frankly, I was skeptical that anything meaningful would actually come from this. I was also, I can admit, a little fearful that I’d learn something I didn’t want to, a fact that might dissolve the little sanity I had left in a year that had already brought its share of unexpected problems.
After filling out an initial health questionnaire, a notification buzzed, forewarning my demise. There are three ways I will likely perish, it said: cardiovascular disease, a sleep disorder, or cancer (it doesn’t specify which type). This means, according to the app, I have already “c
news.summary: Death Clock, an AI-driven longevity app launched in 2024, now offers paid biomarker panels to help users track health metrics and potentially extend life expectancy. The service uses AI trained on longevity studies to generate personalized prevention plans.

news.title: Deepgram acquires Pipecat-maker Daily to bolster its voice AI infrastructure
news.summary_raw: Deepgram said that it is committed to keep Pipecat open source.
news.source_text:
The voice AI sector is hot, and top players are trying to consolidate their position as more business models come to the fore through partnerships and acquisitions. Deepgram is the latest to make such moves: The company said on Thursday that it is acquiring Daily, the maker and maintainer of one of the most popular open-source voice AI infrastructures, Pipecat.
The companies didn’t disclose the deal amount but said that they will keep Pipecat open-source.
For the uninitiated, Pipecat is a framework that manages voice and video streams along with other pieces in the pipeline, like speech-to-text (STT), large language models, and text-to-speech (TTS) models while reducing latency. Its maker, Daily, provides hosted infrastructure for voice and video calls of any kind.
With Pipecat, Deepgram will likely gain a deeper understanding of real-time voice and video infrastructure.
Daily has raised over $62 million in funding to date from investors such as Tiger Global, Highfield Capital, Nat Friedman, Lachy Groom and Kevin Weil, according to PitchBook data. Earlier this year, Deepgram reached unicorn status with a $130 million Series C round. Incidentally, both companies were in the same Y Combinator batch in 2016.
Kwindla Kramer, Daily’s co-founder, said around the time when GPT-4 came out, the company started experimenting with AI-to-human communication over voice and text, which eventually resulted in the Pipecat framework. He noted that while there has been a lot of acquisition interest, he favored Deepgram’s CEO Scott Stephenson’s commitment to keeping Pipecat open-source forever, and the engineering culture of both organizations matched, giving Daily’s team the freedom to work on different parts of the stack within a bigger organization.
“Scott was super committed to Pipecat being open-source and vendor-neutral forever. I think there is both a personal commitment and commercial driver there. If you sit in the middle of an ecosystem that’s growing very fast, and have many parts of that ecosystem that are genuinely the best from your company, then everything being as open as possible is like a commercial advantage,” Kramer told TechCrunch.
Stephenson said that Deepgram has been wanting to work in open source for a long time, and the company realized that an orchestration framework for agents was a potential area, which drove the decision to partner with Daily.
“We want to open up the ecosystem so everybody can build voice agents. It’s great if you’re using Deepgram models, but I want you to be using the best models for your use case. And if Deepgram notices that we have some ground to catch up on in a certain area for our own models and products, that’s great. We want you to use partners, and then we’ll also work on becoming better in those areas,” he said.
Stephenson said the acquisition lets developers build agents with expressivity and end-to-end speech systems by plugging in different models and a context bus that connects all parts.

news.summary: Deepgram has acquired Daily to integrate its Pipecat open‑source voice‑AI framework, expanding Deepgram’s real‑time voice and video processing capabilities. The move positions Deepgram as a more complete end‑to‑end voice AI platform while keeping Pipecat vendor‑neutral and open source.

The Deepgram/Pipecat combo directly impacts any voice‑enabled workflows you maintain, especially if you use third‑party STT/TTS services or build custom voice agents.

news.title: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready
news.source_text:
Protostar Challenge: Climate Risk Intelligence
Manage competition registration, data, and submissions
An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.
The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.
The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.
But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.
Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goa
news.summary: Hugging Face has announced Project ProtoStar, an initiative to standardize publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code into AI‑ready, machine‑actionable formats, aiming to ease reuse and accelerate AI research. The program brings together universities, research organizations, and industry partners to promote open, interoperable scientific artifacts and hosts open challenges to demonstrate their value.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on the ProtoStar challenges starting November 2 as they may provide high‑quality, AI‑ready datasets that could be leveraged for internal training or research projects. Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.
Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

news.title: Read the letter the FBI sent MLK to try to convince him to kill himself (2014)
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://www.vox.com/xpress/2014/11/12/7204453/martin-luther-king-fbi-letter
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50288867
Points: 274
# Comments: 162
news.source_text:
When the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech before huge crowds on the National Mall in August 1963, the FBI took notice.
Read the letter the FBI sent MLK to try to convince him to kill himself
“We must mark him now, if we have not done so before, as the most dangerous Negro of the future in this Nation from the standpoint of communism, the Negro and national security,” FBI Domestic Intelligence Chief William Sullivan wrote in a memo two days later.
A massive surveillance operation on King was quickly approved, and FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover became increasingly fixated on proving that King had communist ties and discrediting him generally.
The surveillance failed to show that King was a communist, but it did result in many tapes of extramarital sexual liaisons by King. So the next year, Sullivan sent the following unsigned letter to King's home. An unredacted version of it was only recently unearthed by Yale historian Beverly Gage, and published in the New York Times in November 2014:
According to Enemies, journalist Tim Weiner's history of the FBI, Sullivan "had a package of the King sex tapes prepared by the FBI's lab technicians," and sent it along with this letter to King's home. The package was opened by King's wife.
“You have been on the record — all your adulterous acts, your sexual orgies extending far into the past. This one is but a tiny sample,” the letter says. It threatens that the public “will know you for what you are — an evil, abnormal beast.” It continues: “Your ‘honorary’ degrees, your Nobel prize (what a grim farce) and other awards will not save you. King, I repeat you are done.”
Though the letter was unsigned and the letter writer appeared to want King to think he was black — "you know you are a complete fraud and a great liability to all of us Negroes," one line states — King and his advisers quickly concluded the letter had been sent by the FBI, Gage writes.
“There is only one thing left for you to do. You know what it is. You have just 34 days,” the letter says, apparently urging King to commit suicide. Fortunately, King didn’t back down. But the letter is a terrifying reminder of what government surveillance agencies can be capable of.
(Hat tip: Catherine Thompson of TPM)
news.summary: The article discusses a 2014 uncovering of an FBI letter allegedly urging Martin Luther King Jr. to commit suicide, highlighting past government surveillance practices.

news.title: A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System
news.summary_raw: Sources tell WIRED that an Accenture employee’s personal Claude agent ran on a DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched.
news.source_text:
Earlier this year, sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent. It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk third-party website.
The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones.
“It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.”
A DOD spokesperson tells WIRED that “the Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems.”
“We take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations,” an Accenture spokesperson tells WIRED. When pressed, Accenture didn’t offer clarification on who conducted the investigation, or dispute that had been what could be characterized as an incident.
The Accenture employee is alleged to have connected a secure production environment to their personal Claude account so as to allow an AI agent to write and deploy code. Claude is currently barred from being used by DOD staff. (Anthropic directed WIRED to the company’s usage policy, which instructs users not to use its products to “interfere with the operation of military bases and related infrastructure” or to “bypass security controls such as authentication systems, end point protection, or monitoring tools without authorization.”)
The Accenture employee’s AI agent ran on the DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Sources indicate that despite the security risks posed by the AI coding agent, Accenture employees did not treat the incident as severe or urgent. DOD employees and federal contractors are required to report any cybersecurity incident within 72 hours of its discovery, but sources indicate Accenture did not initially report the breach to the government at all.
“We are in a conflict with Iran right now,” says the employee, noting that Iran has attempted to hack several federal agencies and parts of US infrastructure. “It’s the wor
news.summary: A contractor used their personal Claude AI coding agent to access a secure Pentagon system, exfiltrating login credentials and sensitive CUI to a third‑party site. The incident exposed a critical vulnerability in the DoD’s authentication controls and highlighted lax reporting by the contractor.

news.title: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
news.source_text:
Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.
The model is released in two official variants:
There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).
Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!
Table of Contents
What is new with Mistral Large 4
Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.
You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.
Cybersecurity Capabilities
Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.
Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.
For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s d

The model’s open‑source licensing and high refusal rate on harmful prompts make it a promising tool for defensive security teams.

news.title: Mistral Says Its AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Has Leapfrogged China in the Open-Weight Race
news.summary_raw: The French AI lab claims its latest release matches or outperforms even the best models from DeepSeek and Z.ai in coding and cybersecurity.
news.source_text:
A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.
The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai.
“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”
The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.
The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)
Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.
Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”
The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.
“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”

news.title: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT
news.summary_raw: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings is buying ADT in a $15.3 billion deal, with plans to bring AI to the home security business.
news.source_text:
Thrive Holdings has acquired physical security company ADT for $10 per share or about $7.6 billion in equity, the companies announced on Thursday. Beyond equity, the total enterprise value of the deal is $15.3 billion, ADT said.
Thrive Holdings is the PE spinout from Josh Kushner’s powerhouse VC firm Thrive Capital. It also counts OpenAI as its partner, as well as an investor. The firm’s mission is to hold other companies long-term, revitalizing them with AI. Currently, Thrive Holdings holds over 75 companies, it says.
As a partner, OpenAI supplies AI models and tech as well as people, otherwise known as forward-deployed engineers, to Thrive’s companies.
Neither ADT nor Thrive announced what new AI-powered security products they will be releasing, but they did tease that the plan was to invest and release new products. “ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business,” the press release said.
AI-powered physical security is having a moment right now. Apple just entered the field with a new line of smart home and home security products in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Amazon updated its smart home line, including new AI-powered home cameras. And who knows what the future might bring? Some startups are offering AI dog robots as roving security guards.

news.title: The ‘Pain in the Ass’ Math That Could Save Vibe Coding From Itself
news.summary_raw: A new startup called &Truth is joining the race to automate formal verification, a painstaking process that uses math to prove software works as intended.
news.source_text:
Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually. The dramatic reduction in time and cost, which Sun reported in a recent paper, is among the early results that are awakening an obscure field of coding and mathematics known as formal verification.
For decades, developers have envisioned using math to prove that their software is bug-free. This process is long and laborious, requiring engineers to write precise statements about the goals of their software and convert their code into formulas that can be validated. While companies already run sophisticated tests to identify as many flaws in their software as possible, they rarely shell out for formal verification, which can catch even more erratic behavior.
Now, a wave of startups is betting that generative AI will make formal software verification both practical and essential. Among them is &Truth, which Sun joined in August and which publicly launched on Thursday. Sun’s research demonstrated the technology’s potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal.
“Bridges, buildings, they don’t collapse, because people did math before constructing them,” says Ilya Sergey, &Truth’s chief science officer. “Why don’t we do the same for code? The technology to mathematically reason was all there, just difficult to scale.”
&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Rival Harmonic, which was cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and has received $295 million in funding, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. It is evaluating the technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia, whose venture capital arm is one of the startup’s investors.
And just last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced they had used AI to assist in finding bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect. They also introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification. Costs of the initial project were not disclosed.
The big promise is a future where software runs more reliably with fewer security headaches. But whether AI can bring formal verification beyond the most critical systems at organizations like NASA and Apple and into widespread use remains an open question.
The technology is still in the prototyping stage. Though demand is high, it’s unclear how much customers are willing to pay and how they prefer to adopt the technology. Formal verification relies on making assumptions about how computers and people interact with software, and some experts are skeptical about its ability to catch bugs stemming from user erro
news.summary: Stanford researchers unveiled &Truth, an AI-powered formal verification tool that completed a complex engineering project in under 12 hours for less than $500, a drastic improvement over traditional methods. The startup, backed by $70M, aims to extend AI-driven verification to all programming languages, promising more reliable code with fewer security flaws.

news.title: As search traffic dries up, Reddit announces it’s shifting to a logged-in experience
news.summary_raw: As AI transforms how people find information online, Reddit is rethinking its open-web roots to protect its audience and business.
news.source_text:
Reddit has long attracted millions of users to its site through Google, with many even appending the word “Reddit” to their search queries for better answers. But as search traffic dries up amid the shift to AI-powered search, Reddit is rethinking its relationship with the open internet. In its third-quarter earnings call on Thursday, the company announced it’s transitioning to a primarily “logged-in experience.”
The move is designed to protect its data from AI scraping, allowing the company to instead forge lucrative licensing deals with model providers. But just as important, such a shift could help Reddit to increase its revenue even as it faces daily active user declines in its largest market, the U.S.
Overall, Reddit’s global daily active users were flat quarter-over-quarter in Q3, reaching 130.3 million, while U.S. daily active users dropped from 53.2 million in Q2 to 50.7 million in Q3 and were down 2% year-over-year.
The company is not alone in seeing such declines; the shift to an AI-centered web has impacted most websites and publishers by now, leading to fewer click-throughs, as AI summaries provide answers that don’t require website visits and Google’s traditional “ten blue links” have reduced relevance. (The change is now even impacting Google’s bottom line, its earnings revealed.)
But at Reddit’s scale, the numbers associated with such a decline are enormous. The company said search traffic referrals dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week in October. It warned that if the trend continues, daily active users could decline to a low-double-digit percentage by next quarter. (To play that out: a hypothetical 10% to 12% decline could bring Reddit to roughly 115 million to 117 million daily actives, down from 130.3 million in Q3. That’s a huge drop!)
At the same time, Reddit has gotten significantly better at monetizing its audience even as its growth weakens. Revenue increased 53% year-over-year to $895 million, ahead of Wall Street’s expectations of about $875 million. Net income rose 74% to $283 million. Advertising revenue grew 54% to $847 million while nonadvertising revenue, which includes its AI data-licensing business, grew 35% year-over-year to $48 million.
And despite a 2% year-over-year decline in U.S. daily users, Reddit’s average revenue per daily active user in the U.S. rose 53% to $13.82. Globally, average revenue per daily active user increased 36% year-over-year to $6.87.
Shifting to a logged-in experience could boost those numbers even higher because logged-in users are typically worth more to advertisers.
Unlike the logged-out users who often find their way to the site via search, logged-in users provide more signals about their interests and behaviors, which helps to better target and personalize ads.
Those same signals would also help Reddit provide a more personalized experience to its users, which includes personalized feeds, recommendations of new communities to subscribe to, and pushes to vote
news.summary: Reddit is transitioning to a primarily logged‑in user experience to protect its data from AI scraping and to strengthen its monetization through licensing deals. This shift reflects broader industry moves toward limiting AI‑driven search traffic and increasing direct user engagement.
